questions.prompt: The reference, larger-mass, and stiffer-spring rows start side by side. Explain how their relative cycle counts over the same viewing interval separate inertia from restoring action.
questions.answer: The reference uses m and K. Increasing mass to 4m with K fixed slows the motion to half the reference rate because the same restoring action changes a heavier mass’s motion more slowly. Increasing effective stiffness to 4K with m fixed doubles the reference rate because the return toward equilibrium is stronger. Comparing cycles over the same interval distinguishes the rate changes from different displacement sizes.
rubric: Hold stiffness fixed when interpreting the larger-mass row and mass fixed when interpreting the stiffer row.
Explain half-rate versus twice-rate through inertia and restoring action, rather than the drawing’s size.

questions.prompt: A student replaces the transverse spring segments with axially stiffer ones but leaves their tension and geometry unchanged. Why is this a different manipulation from increasing the effective transverse K in the demonstration?
questions.answer: K denotes restoring stiffness in the displayed motion direction. The transverse return depends on the pre-tension and geometry of the segments, rather than simply the axial spring constant considered in isolation. The demonstration explicitly matches the transverse restoring coefficient to the longitudinal one. Changing an axial property without establishing a larger restoring effect across the spring line does not establish the same frequency prediction.
rubric: Identify K as effective stiffness in the motion direction.
Distinguish changing axial spring constant from establishing a larger transverse restoring effect.

questions.prompt: An animation frame catches all the masses on their equilibrium marks. What extra observation would distinguish an instant of zero displacement from a displacement node?
questions.answer: Follow the same location through the motion. A moving mass can cross equilibrium for an instant and then continue to the other side. A displacement node in a pure mode remains at equilibrium throughout that mode’s oscillation. One frame cannot establish that persistent condition.
rubric: Distinguish momentary zero displacement from persistent zero displacement.
Require observing the same location across phases of the specified mode.
questions.topic: A node versus an equilibrium crossing

questions.prompt: In the three-mass comparison, describe the relationship among the outer masses and the middle mass in the lowest and highest modes. Why does counting the physical masses not distinguish those two rows?
questions.answer: The same three masses appear in both rows. In the lowest mode they move together, with the middle mass making the largest excursion. In the highest mode the outer masses move together while the middle mass moves oppositely. The changing relative pattern alters the deformation of their couplings, so a different coordinated pattern and rate can occur without adding or removing masses.
rubric: Describe together-motion in the lowest mode and middle-versus-ends opposition in the highest.
Keep the physical system fixed while attributing the difference to coordinated pattern.
questions.topic: Comparing the first and third modes

questions.prompt: How would you use several phases of these ideal undamped animations to check whether a mode is fading, rather than judging from one nearly flat frame?
questions.answer: Compare the largest excursions reached in successive cycles of the same mode. A nearly flat frame can be an equilibrium crossing within an oscillation that later returns to its full excursion. The source models undamped motion, so the excursion should not progressively shrink from cycle to cycle. Looking across phases separates that recurring crossing from a fading amplitude.
rubric: Compare successive cycle maxima instead of one frame.
Connect the undamped assumption to continuing excursion without progressive decay.

questions.prompt: The atlas has an empty cell in the three-mass row under mode 5. Explain the empty cell and the physical information carried by a row, without treating the blank as a missing video.
questions.answer: A row specifies how many masses can move in the displayed direction. Three moving masses provide three independent modes, so modes 4 and 5 do not belong in that row. Rows with more moving masses have more available patterns, producing the triangular layout. The blank indicates a pattern outside that system’s mode count rather than an unplayed phase.
rubric: Read row labels as moving-mass count.
Explain the triangular layout using the available mode count in each row.

questions.prompt: The atlas scales each pattern to the same maximum displayed displacement. What comparison is this choice useful for, and what amplitude comparison would it make misleading?
questions.answer: The shared visual scale helps compare where masses move together or oppositely and where reversals occur along a row. It does not show the naturally excited amplitude of one mode relative to another, because those displayed maxima were deliberately matched. A taller-looking local part must be interpreted within the scaled pattern rather than as evidence that its physical mode was excited more strongly.
rubric: Identify spatial-pattern comparison as the purpose of normalization.
Avoid inferring relative natural excitation from matched displayed maxima.

questions.prompt: The five fixed–fixed rows have different numbers of lobes, yet the supports do not change. Explain how higher modes can differ internally while satisfying the same endpoint requirement.
questions.answer: Both endpoints stay at zero displacement in every row. Higher modes fit additional alternating half-waves between those same supports, introducing internal locations of zero displacement and regions moving oppositely. The interior pattern can therefore become more complex while preserving the fixed ends. Under the ideal string conditions, those shorter spatial patterns have higher frequencies.
rubric: Keep both endpoint displacements zero for every mode.
Connect additional internal half-waves and reversals with a higher mode under the same boundary conditions.

questions.prompt: Design a comparison that isolates the effect of freeing one endpoint. Which conditions should remain matched, and which feature of the result should be measured?
questions.answer: Use the same ideal string length and wave speed, changing the endpoint condition from fixed to free while retaining the other fixed end. Measure the fundamental frequency in each condition rather than retuning both examples to the same displayed frequency. Under those matched conditions, the fixed–free fundamental is half the fixed–fixed fundamental. Separate retuning would obscure the boundary effect.
rubric: Hold length and wave speed fixed while changing one endpoint.
Measure the fundamental and distinguish the matched comparison from separately retuned illustrations.

questions.prompt: The combined string is labeled “Same string, all at once.” Explain how the separate mode panels determine one spatial displacement pattern, rather than representing five independent physical strings.
questions.answer: The panels isolate five possible contributions to the motion of the same string. At each position and instant, their signed displacements are added to obtain the displacement of that point in the combined field. Different positions receive different combinations because each mode has its own spatial shape. The bottom panel is therefore one changing string shape formed by superposition, not five strings occupying separate copies of the space.
rubric: Interpret the separate panels as contributions to one physical string.
Explain addition of signed displacement at each position and instant to form the full field.

A cycle counted directly in playback time is a slowed display cycle, not a 100 Hz physical cycle occurring at normal speed.

The (2,1) pattern divides twice along the first direction and once along the other, while (1,2) exchanges those roles. The numbers describe shape, not frequencies in Hz. The illustration assigns the displayed frequencies separately, and its natural eigenfrequencies should not be inferred from those pair labels alone.

questions.prompt: The combined membrane panel looks vertically flatter than an individual-mode panel. Why would that picture alone be a poor test of whether adding the modes weakened the motion?
questions.answer: The combined surface is displayed at a reduced vertical scale so it fits in its panel. Its apparent height therefore cannot be compared directly with the magnified individual panels. The physical mixture is the sum of their contributions, while the drawing’s scale is a separate representational choice. Compare values or drawings on a shared scale before inferring weaker motion.

questions.prompt: At one marked mass and one instant, the two contributing modes have equal displacements in opposite directions. Explain why zero displacement in their sum at that instant does not mean either mode has been removed.
questions.answer: The simultaneous contributions cancel at that mass at that instant. Each mode continues to oscillate at its own rate, so their relative contributions can change afterward and cancellation can disappear. A temporary zero in the sum is different from deleting a component or establishing a persistent node of the whole motion.
rubric: Apply addition to the simultaneous opposite displacements.
Keep temporary local cancellation distinct from removing a mode or making a permanent node.

questions.prompt: Suppose a carefully measured laryngeal signal has nearly equally spaced peaks. Explain what this would support and what it would leave unsettled about the membrane model.
questions.answer: The hypothetical measurement would support the specific predicted regular spacing for that signal under those recording conditions. questions.answer: No. The prediction concerns gaps between the peak frequencies, not equality of their amplitudes. questions.prompt: Teal and orange distinguish individual masses in the two-mass comparison, but an entire atlas mode is drawn in one color. Which reading respects these different legends?

options.text: Color identifies individual masses in the paired comparison but mode number in the atlas, so its meaning follows the local legend.
options.feedback: The color code changes role across the two figures. Reading each local legend prevents treating all equally colored atlas masses as one physical mass.

options.text: Treat orange as the second physical mass throughout both figures, so every orange atlas point marks a duplicate view of that same moving element.

options.text: Treat color as displacement direction in both figures, so a teal mass cannot move in the opposite direction from another teal mass.

questions.prompt: In the fixed–fixed amplitude spectrum, what would moving a plotted peak upward without changing its horizontal position represent?

options.text: A higher frequency for the same mode, because the spectrum uses vertical distance to indicate how many cycles occur per second.
options.feedback: Frequency is horizontal in this spectrum, not vertical.

options.text: A longer string displacement wavelength, because spectral height counts the distance between successive spatial nodes.
options.feedback: The vertical spectral axis is not a spatial coordinate or a node-spacing measure.

options.text: A larger measured contribution at the same frequency, rather than a faster mode or an added spatial half-wave.

options.text: A larger displacement of the complete string at every point, because one peak’s height specifies the spatial excursion of the entire mixture.
options.feedback: A spectral height describes one frequency contribution at the pickup, not the total displacement at every position on the string.

questions.answer: The vertical axis is amplitude, whereas horizontal position specifies frequency. A height change does not itself change mode rate or the spatial pattern.
rubric: Read vertical displacement in the graph as amplitude.

questions.prompt: The ideal fixed–fixed sequence shows one through five half-waves at 100 through 500 Hz. What should the next allowed pattern in that same ideal sequence add?

options.text: A free antinode at one end, because a fixed–fixed string must change endpoint type after five spatial divisions have been fitted.
options.feedback: The displayed five modes are not a physical limit of the ideal string. Higher modes can retain both fixed endpoints.

options.text: A second physical string, because fitting a sixth half-wave exceeds the number of available moving points in the continuous system.

questions.answer: An additional half-wave preserves fixed endpoints in the ideal continuous string. The sequence continues to the sixth harmonic rather than changing boundary type.

questions.prompt: Suppose a pickup is placed at a displacement node of one excited string mode while other modes still move there. What is the best interpretation of a missing contribution from that mode in the local measurement?

options.text: The mode has been removed physically from the string, so every other point must now share the pickup’s zero displacement for that frequency.
options.feedback: A local node does not eliminate the mode’s displacement elsewhere.

options.text: The pickup is insensitive to that mode’s displacement at that location; its absence from this local signal does not show that the whole string has lost that mode.
options.feedback: A mode can have zero displacement at the chosen point while moving elsewhere. Measurement location affects visibility of a contribution without deleting the system’s mode.

options.text: The mode’s frequency has shifted to the nearest remaining peak, because measuring at a node changes the boundary conditions of the undisturbed string.
options.feedback: The hypothetical observation changes pickup location, not the undisturbed string’s endpoint conditions or mode frequencies.

options.text: The missing height should be interpreted as negative amplitude and added to a different peak, because the spectrum preserves the number of visible modes by reassigning them.

questions.answer: A mode can have zero displacement at the chosen point while moving elsewhere. Measurement location affects visibility of a contribution without deleting the system’s mode.
rubric: Connect a local node with zero measured displacement from that mode.

questions.topic: A mode hidden at a pickup location

questions.prompt: Which displacement description satisfies the stated endpoint conditions of the fixed–free string?

options.text: The bottom remains at zero displacement while the top can undergo a large excursion as a free-end antinode.
options.feedback: The fixed bottom is a displacement node and the free top is an antinode in the illustrated modes.

options.text: Both endpoints remain at zero displacement, so the free top is identified by its lack of movement over a complete cycle.

options.text: The bottom makes the largest excursion while the top remains still, reversing the two endpoint roles as the string completes each cycle.

options.text: Both endpoints move with the interior, with fixed and free referring to whether a spectral peak is drawn rather than to physical displacement.

questions.answer: The fixed bottom is a displacement node and the free top is an antinode in the illustrated modes.
rubric: Identify the displacement node at the fixed end.

questions.prompt: The fixed–free diagram calls its 300 Hz pattern mode 2 even though the displayed fundamental is 100 Hz. Why are those two labels compatible?

options.text: Mode 2 counts two cycles per second, while 300 Hz counts the number of spatial peaks drawn in the same pattern.
options.feedback: Mode number is not a cycle-per-second unit, and Hz refers to temporal frequency rather than spatial peak count.

options.text: Mode 2 identifies the second physical mass, while 300 Hz is the rate assigned to that mass independently of the rest of the string.
options.feedback: The diagram describes a continuous string’s coordinated patterns, not separately assigned mass rates.

options.text: Mode 2 counts the second allowed pattern, while 300 Hz is the third harmonic; the even-multiple pattern between them does not satisfy these endpoints.
options.feedback: Mode order counts allowed patterns. The fixed–free ideal sequence contains odd harmonics, so its second mode is the third harmonic.

options.text: Mode 2 means the second harmonic, so the 300 Hz label must be reinterpreted as an amplitude value to preserve the numbering.
options.feedback: Frequency and mode order have distinct meanings. The source labels 300 Hz as frequency, not amplitude.

questions.answer: Mode order counts allowed patterns. The fixed–free ideal sequence contains odd harmonics, so its second mode is the third harmonic.
rubric: Separate allowed-mode order from harmonic number.
Relate the distinction to odd-multiple fixed–free modes.

questions.prompt: An otherwise ideal fixed–free example is retuned so its lowest frequency is 200 Hz. Which list preserves the relationship among its first four allowed frequencies?

options.text: 200, 400, 600, and 800 Hz, preserving consecutive multiples because a different base removes the effect of the free endpoint.
options.feedback: Changing the base does not replace the fixed–free odd-multiple sequence with the fixed–fixed sequence.

options.text: 200, 300, 500, and 700 Hz, changing the lowest value while leaving the higher frequencies tied to the original illustration.
options.feedback: Retuning the ideal sequence changes its shared frequency scale rather than replacing only one label.

options.text: 100, 300, 500, and 700 Hz, keeping the original frequencies because endpoint type fixes their numerical values independently of tuning.

options.text: 200, 600, 1000, and 1400 Hz, preserving the first, third, fifth, and seventh multiples of its own lowest frequency.

questions.answer: Retuning the base changes the frequency scale while the ideal fixed–free boundary pattern retains odd multiples.
rubric: Preserve odd multiples relative to the new base.
Distinguish frequency ratios from one demonstration’s numerical tuning.

questions.prompt: The membrane has complicated interior patterns, including the four-region (2,2) example. What remains shared across its displayed individual-mode panels?

options.text: The center remains fixed in each mode, so the interior subdivisions merely show different ways of drawing one central displacement node.
options.feedback: The first membrane pattern has a moving interior. Fixed outer edges do not imply a stationary center in every mode.

options.text: The entire outer edge remains fixed even though the interior can divide into different moving regions.
options.feedback: The common boundary constrains the edge displacement, while the interior patterns differ between modes.

options.text: One outer edge becomes free for each added interior division, so the higher-mode panels use progressively different boundary types.
options.feedback: The source specifies fixed edges across the membrane examples.

options.text: The interior moves as a rigid sheet with one displacement, and the apparent subdivisions indicate different spectral-peak amplitudes rather than spatial motion.
options.feedback: The drawn mode shapes have distinct spatial regions moving differently. They are not rigid-sheet translations.

questions.answer: The common boundary constrains the edge displacement, while the interior patterns differ between modes.

questions.prompt: A string illustration and a membrane illustration both show five equally spaced, equal-height spectral peaks. What further evidence would help distinguish the represented systems rather than treating those spectra as complete descriptions?

options.text: Inspect the spatial motion and boundary geometry as well as the spectra, since a single-point spectrum does not display whether the moving medium is a line or a surface.
options.feedback: The string and membrane have different spatial fields and boundaries despite their deliberately similar spectral examples. The membrane frequencies are assigned for the illustration, so matching spectra do not establish identical natural systems.

options.text: Compare peak heights as a map of spatial nodes, treating equal amplitudes at matching frequencies as enough to establish the same interior motion pattern.
options.feedback: Single-point spectral amplitudes are not a spatial map of nodes. Matching them does not establish identical interior mode shapes or geometry.

options.text: Inspect the highest label as a physical mass count, since a 500 Hz fifth peak determines that the moving medium contains five discrete masses.
options.feedback: A frequency label does not specify a count of physical masses, and these are extended-media illustrations.

options.feedback: The membrane gaps are assigned. Matching them does not establish the same natural spatial or frequency structure.

questions.answer: The string and membrane have different spatial fields and boundaries despite their deliberately similar spectral examples. The membrane frequencies are assigned for the illustration, so matching spectra do not establish identical natural systems.

questions.prompt: The lecture moves from a differential-equation account to a prediction and then proposes a recording. Which role does the prediction play in that sequence?

options.text: It supplies a measured outcome already contained in the equation, so recording adds an illustration without providing evidence that can disagree with the model.
options.feedback: A model’s consequence is not already an observed outcome. Measurement can test whether the consequence matches the signal.

options.text: It chooses the recording result after the spectrum has been inspected, so agreement follows from adjusting the predicted claim to whichever peaks appear.
options.feedback: That reverses the intended role of a specified testable prediction.

options.text: It states a measurable consequence of the model, allowing the recorded signal to be compared with something specified before the result is known.
options.feedback: A prediction connects the account of change to an observable consequence. The proposed recording can then test that consequence rather than merely repeat the theory’s wording.

options.text: It allows the assigned membrane animation to confirm the predicted spacing independently, with the recording used to illustrate a result already established by the schematic.
options.feedback: Assigned frequencies in a model illustration are not independent measurement evidence for its prediction. The recording is proposed to test the signal, not merely to repeat an established result.

questions.answer: A prediction connects the account of change to an observable consequence. The proposed recording can then test that consequence rather than merely repeat the theory’s wording.
rubric: Identify the prediction as an observable model consequence.

questions.topic: The role of a testable prediction

questions.prompt: Suppose a suitable hypothetical laryngeal recording has clearly unequal gaps between several successive spectral peaks. Which conclusion follows for the stated regular-spacing prediction under those conditions?

options.text: The prediction is supported if the peaks have equal heights, because equal amplitude can substitute for equal frequency gaps when evaluating harmonic spacing.
options.feedback: Amplitude equality is a different property and does not establish the predicted regular frequency spacing.

options.text: The prediction is supported by the existence of several peaks, since the count of components carries the same information as the distances between them.
options.feedback: A multi-peak spectrum can have unequal gaps. Component count does not establish regular spacing.

options.text: The prediction has been confirmed for other participants by the assigned animation, so the measured gaps can be treated as irrelevant to evaluating it.
options.feedback: The animation is not participant evidence, and the hypothetical measurement directly addresses the predicted spacing.

options.text: The observed spacing does not match the prediction for that recording; different peak heights would not by themselves resolve a mismatch in frequency gaps.
options.feedback: The predicted quantity is frequency spacing. Unequal observed gaps would count against that specific prediction under the tested conditions, without establishing a universal conclusion about all speakers or membranes.

questions.answer: The predicted quantity is frequency spacing. Unequal observed gaps would count against that specific prediction under the tested conditions, without establishing a universal conclusion about all speakers or membranes.
rubric: Compare the hypothetical gap pattern with the stated prediction.
Avoid substituting amplitude, count, or assigned schematic values for measured frequency spacing.

questions.prompt: In the air-chain model, a pair of neighboring air elements moves closer together and later farther apart. Explain what the masses and springs represent and why the change does not require new air particles to appear.
questions.answer: The masses stand for moving portions of air, while the spring-like connections represent the restoring response to changes in spacing. Bringing neighbors closer compresses the same air, and separating them produces rarefaction. The model changes particle positions and distances, rather than creating a new set of particles for each phase. This physical movement is longitudinal along the tube.
rubric: Identify moving air elements and a restoring effect associated with changed spacing.
Explain compression and rarefaction through changing distances among the same elements.

questions.prompt: A local constriction produces almost no measured frequency change in one mode. A student concludes that neither local mass nor local stiffness changed. Why is that conclusion stronger than the evidence supports?
questions.answer: A small frequency change does not identify the individual mechanical changes. The mode may participate weakly in the altered region, or the downward mass contribution and upward stiffness contribution may partly oppose one another. The observation therefore does not establish that both properties stayed unchanged. Examining the local motion and deformation, or isolating mass and stiffness changes in controlled comparisons, would distinguish these possibilities.
rubric: Explain why a near-zero net shift does not establish unchanged mass and stiffness.
Identify weak local participation or opposing contributions and propose evidence that would distinguish them.

questions.prompt: Design a test of the claim that a given mode is more sensitive to added mass at one location than at another. What should stay the same, what should change, and what should you measure?
questions.answer: Use the same system and excite the same identifiable mode in a reference condition. Add the same small mass at the first location, measure that mode’s frequency change, restore the reference, and repeat at the second location. Hold the underlying stiffness, boundary conditions and measurement procedure fixed. Compare the shifts with how strongly the unperturbed mode moves at each location, expecting the larger downward shift where its motion is larger.
rubric: Keep the system, tested mode and added mass comparable while changing location.
Measure frequency changes against the same reference and relate their sizes to local modal motion.

questions.prompt: Suppose you are given the shape of a vowel that is not one of the three worked examples. Explain the steps needed to predict its first two formant changes without assuming that every constriction behaves like /u/.
questions.answer: Locate the constriction along the glottis-to-lips direction and compare that region with each of the first two mode patterns of the reference system. Determine whether local air motion or local compression and springiness dominates for each mode. A mass-dominated response favors a decrease, while a stiffness-dominated response favors an increase. The worked vowels demonstrate this reasoning method, but their direction pairs cannot simply be assigned to a different constriction without checking its location and modal participation.
rubric: Locate the constriction relative to the glottis and lips.
Assess motion versus deformation separately for the first two modes before predicting their directions.

questions.prompt: You want to compare two string conditions using the heights of their spectral peaks. Why should you keep the pickup location and way of exciting the modes controlled, rather than treating every height change as a changed resonance frequency?
questions.answer: A measured peak’s height depends on how strongly its mode is excited and how much that mode moves at the pickup location. The lecture deliberately selects modal amplitudes so that the five peaks are equal at one marked point. Changing the excitation or pickup can therefore change peak heights without moving the underlying mode frequencies. A controlled comparison should keep those factors fixed and distinguish horizontal frequency shifts from vertical amplitude changes.
rubric: Explain how excitation and local pickup displacement affect peak heights.
Distinguish a change in measured amplitude from a shift in the mode frequency.

questions.prompt: A student expects the three-mass system to have frequencies in the ratio 1:2:3 because it has three modes. Use the lecture’s discrete and continuous examples to explain why that expectation fails.
questions.answer: Three moving masses give three independent modes, but the number of modes does not set their frequency ratios. The illustrated equal-mass chain has ratios near 1, 1.848 and 2.414. Integer harmonics belong to the ideal continuous fixed–fixed string under its boundary and wave assumptions. Transferring that rule to a finite chain confuses two different kinds of system.
rubric: Separate the count of independent modes from their frequency ratios.
Use the noninteger three-mass ratios and identify the different assumptions behind the continuous string’s integer harmonics.

questions.prompt: A system can support several modes, but a one-point displacement recording has fewer clear spectral peaks. Give two source-based reasons why the peak count alone is not a reliable count of all the modes the system can support.
questions.answer: The recording contains the modes that are excited and contribute motion at the chosen pickup, rather than a list of every mode the system could support. An unexcited mode contributes no measured component, and a mode with little or no displacement at that point contributes a weak or absent displacement peak. Changing excitation or pickup can reveal additional components without adding another moving mass or creating another supported mode.
rubric: Separate supported modes from excited and locally measured components.
Identify both excitation and pickup participation as reasons for fewer peaks.

questions.prompt: In the two-mode mixture, one mass sometimes moves less than it does in either pure-mode drawing. Explain how that can happen while the physical mass and spring properties remain unchanged.
questions.answer: The mixed displacement is the sum of the two modal contributions at that instant. When the contributions at a mass point in opposite directions, they partly cancel, giving a smaller net displacement. When they point in the same direction, they reinforce. The changing resultant motion comes from adding the existing mode motions, not from repeatedly changing the mass or coupling stiffness.
rubric: Explain the mixed displacement as an instantaneous sum of modal contributions.
Connect smaller motion to cancellation and larger motion to reinforcement without changing mechanical properties.

questions.prompt: Treat this as a hypothetical experiment: repeated, well-controlled measurements of steady laryngeal vibration fail to show the predicted evenly spaced peaks. What would that mean for the stated prediction, and why could the assigned-frequency membrane animation not override the measurements?
questions.answer: That result would count against the stated prediction under the measured conditions and would call for reconsidering the model, its assumptions or its scope. The membrane animation is constructed with illustrative harmonic frequencies, so its evenly spaced peaks follow from that assignment rather than independent measurement of a natural membrane. A demonstration can make a prediction understandable, but it cannot substitute for the experimental evidence used to test it.
rubric: Interpret the hypothetical result as a challenge to the prediction under the tested conditions.
Distinguish deliberately assigned animation frequencies from independent measured evidence.

questions.prompt: The mode atlas scales different panels to similar maximum visible displacement, and the membrane mixture uses a reduced vertical scale. Why would ranking frequencies by the tallest-looking drawing be a poor interpretation of these displays?
questions.answer: Visible height represents displacement after the chosen drawing scale, not how many cycles occur per second. Normalizing the atlas amplitudes helps compare spatial patterns, while reducing the membrane mixture’s scale keeps the summed motion inside its panel. Neither adjustment sets the mode frequency. Frequency should be read from the labels or compared using cycles over the same time interval, with the stated playback slowing taken into account.
rubric: Separate visible displacement scale from temporal oscillation rate.
Use the stated normalization and mixture scaling to explain why panel height cannot rank frequencies.

questions.prompt: Why is the free endpoint a useful displacement pickup for the illustrated fixed–free string mixture, while the fixed endpoint would be a poor pickup for that same purpose?
questions.answer: The fixed endpoint is a displacement node for each allowed mode, so measuring displacement there misses their motion. The free endpoint is a displacement antinode for the illustrated modes, so each contributes a strong displacement signal there. With equal excitation in the demonstration, the free-end mixture has four equal-height spectral peaks. The measurement position helps explain the observed spectrum without changing which modes the string supports.
rubric: Use node versus antinode behavior to compare the endpoints as displacement pickups.
Connect free-end measurement and equal excitation to the illustrated spectrum.

questions.prompt: Explain how the simplified glottis-to-lips air chain can be compared with a fixed–free system even though its particles move longitudinally and the string picture moves transversely.
questions.answer: The comparison depends on the boundary constraints and patterns of displacement, not on drawing the particles along the same path. The simplified glottal end constrains displacement, while the open lip end allows strong motion. Longitudinal air motion can therefore have fixed–free-like mode patterns with the first two uniform-tube resonances in an odd-multiple relationship. The transverse string is an analogy for those constraints, not a claim that air particles follow the curved string outline.
rubric: Identify the constrained glottal end and motion-permitting lip end in the simplified model.
Separate the common boundary-pattern principle from the different physical directions of motion.

questions.prompt: A measured constriction lowers F1 and raises F2. Why is that result consistent with the illustrated /i/ account without by itself proving that the constriction was exactly two-thirds of the way from the glottis?
questions.answer: The direction pair agrees with a mass-dominated first-mode response and a stiffness-dominated second-mode response in the /i/ example. However, a pair of frequency changes is an outcome, not a direct measurement of constriction position. To support the proposed location and mechanism, compare the actual articulatory shape with the reference and examine how the relevant modes move and deform in that region. The example supplies a supported explanation, rather than a unique location-reading rule from two arrows alone.
rubric: Recognize agreement with the illustrated /i/ direction pair.
Separate consistency with an account from direct evidence for the exact location, and name the needed spatial evidence.
questions.topic: Inferring a mechanism from formant shifts

questions.prompt: The air-column display isolates Mode1@F1, Mode2@F2 and Mode3@F3 in separate rows. Explain how to read those rows without treating them as three separate air streams passing through the vocal tract.
questions.answer: Each row isolates a possible resonance pattern of the same air system so its local movement and compression can be examined. Higher modes contain more alternating spatial regions along the same tube. A physical vibration can combine modal contributions, just as the mechanical mixtures add motions in one system. The separate rows are a way to study the components, rather than three independent streams that occupy different tracts.
rubric: Treat the rows as isolated mode patterns of one air system.
Explain why spatial differences and possible superposition do not imply separate physical air streams.
questions.topic: One air system with several resonances

questions.prompt: The reference row has frequency 0.5 Hz, the 4m row 0.25 Hz, and the 4K row 1 Hz. Explain the order of these rates and why it agrees in both motion directions without doing a formula calculation.
questions.answer: The heavier mass changes its motion more slowly under the unchanged restoring effect, so its cycle lasts longest and its frequency is lowest. The stronger effective stiffness changes the same mass’s motion more rapidly, so its cycle is shortest and its frequency is highest. The reference lies between them. Longitudinal and transverse examples have the same rate ordering because the comparison matches the effective restoring stiffness in the relevant motion direction.
rubric: Explain lower rate for greater mass and higher rate for greater effective stiffness through changes in motion.
Relate the matching directional comparisons to effective stiffness rather than visual direction alone.

questions.prompt: In the economic stabilization illustration, the unemployment and inflation curves have peaks and troughs that are pressed flatter. What shared dynamical idea connects that picture to the course, and what would be missing if you tried to use the picture alone as a quantitative prediction?
questions.answer: The shared idea is that a system can fluctuate over time and that changing how it operates can reduce the size of those fluctuations. Flattening the peaks and troughs depicts stabilization, with the caption linking it to avoiding high unemployment or runaway inflation. The illustration does not provide the actual governing relationships, parameter values or measurements needed to calculate a policy’s outcome. It communicates an aim and a pattern of change rather than a complete quantitative model.
rubric: Identify stabilization as reducing fluctuations over time.
Distinguish the illustration’s conceptual pattern from the missing relationships and data needed for quantitative prediction.

questions.prompt: For the ideal two-equal-mass chain, propose what would happen if you increased only the middle coupling’s stiffness. Which pure mode should be more sensitive, and how does the relative movement of its two masses support your prediction?
questions.answer: In the first mode the two masses move together by equal amounts, so their separation does not change and the middle coupling has little deformation. In the second mode they move oppositely, strongly changing that separation and stretching or compressing the middle coupling. A small stiffness increase there should therefore raise the second mode’s frequency more strongly, while leaving the ideal in-phase pattern much less affected. The prediction uses deformation in the chosen coupling, not merely the displacement of an individual mass.
rubric: Compare relative displacement across the middle coupling in the two pure modes.
Predict greater upward stiffness sensitivity for the oppositely moving mode.
questions.topic: A local-stiffness prediction in a small chain

questions.prompt: What is physically different about the membrane patterns labelled (2,1), (1,2) and (2,2), and why are those pairs not simply another way to name the second, third and fourth harmonic frequencies?
questions.answer: The two entries describe divisions along two different directions of the membrane surface. The (2,1) pattern has two half-wave divisions along one direction and one along the other, while (1,2) exchanges those roles. The (2,2) pattern divides both directions. These pairs describe spatial shape. The demonstration separately assigns its displayed frequencies for illustration, so reading the pair as a harmonic-frequency multiplier would confuse a two-dimensional shape label with a frequency claim.
rubric: Describe how the two indices distinguish spatial divisions in two surface directions.
Separate those shape labels from the deliberately assigned illustrative frequencies.

questions.prompt: The longitudinal and transverse one-mass examples oscillate at the same rate. Which explanation fits the conditions of this comparison?

options.text: Their rates match because the same visible travel distance fixes the cycle time, even if the effective restoring strengths of the two arrangements differ.
options.feedback: Equal travel distance does not establish equal frequency. This comparison matches mass and total restoring stiffness, and its transverse amplitudes are enlarged for visibility.

options.text: Their mass and total restoring stiffness in the displayed direction are matched, so changing the direction of motion does not change the rate in these models.
options.feedback: The model matches mass and total effective restoring stiffness. Its two pre-tensioned transverse segments each supply half the reference restoring coefficient, producing the same 0.5 Hz rate.

options.text: Their rates match because each transverse segment supplies the full longitudinal stiffness, giving two complete restoring effects that compensate for the changed direction.
options.feedback: The transverse segments each contribute half the effective restoring stiffness in this model. Together they match the longitudinal total, rather than doubling it.

options.text: Their rates match because a longitudinal spring and a transverse spring have the same restoring action whenever they are drawn with an equal number of coils.
options.feedback: The relevant quantity is effective restoring stiffness in the direction of motion. Coil count in a drawing does not establish that match.

questions.answer: The model matches mass and total effective restoring stiffness. Its two pre-tensioned transverse segments each supply half the reference restoring coefficient, producing the same 0.5 Hz rate.
rubric: Identify matched mass and effective restoring stiffness.
Keep the conclusion conditional on the stated model comparison.
questions.topic: Why directional examples have matching rates

questions.prompt: Lecture 12’s summary line prints stiffness increasing with frequency decreasing, but its later principle and the controlled comparison point the other way. Which interpretation should guide a prediction at fixed mass?

options.text: Increasing stiffness lowers frequency, because returning more strongly toward equilibrium makes the mass stay near its resting point for a longer part of each cycle.
options.feedback: A stronger restoring effect makes the undamped cycle quicker. Remaining close to equilibrium is an amplitude idea and does not explain a slower rate here.

options.text: Increasing stiffness leaves frequency unchanged, because a stiffness change can alter visible excursion while mass supplies the entire timing of an oscillation.
options.feedback: The controlled comparison changes effective stiffness at fixed mass and changes the rate. Both mass and restoring stiffness matter.

options.text: Increasing stiffness first lowers frequency until the mass reaches equilibrium, after which the frequency rises during the return part of the same cycle.
options.feedback: The mode has a characteristic rate under fixed parameters. Its rate is not assigned opposite stiffness effects on successive parts of the cycle.

options.text: Increasing effective restoring stiffness raises frequency, because the same moving mass is returned toward equilibrium more strongly and completes cycles more quickly.
options.feedback: At fixed mass, greater effective restoring stiffness raises frequency. The controlled 4K comparison oscillates faster, and Lecture 13 explicitly corrects the summary arrow.

questions.answer: At fixed mass, greater effective restoring stiffness raises frequency. The controlled 4K comparison oscillates faster, and Lecture 13 explicitly corrects the summary arrow.
rubric: Apply the controlled stiffness comparison rather than the typographical arrow.
Explain the direction through a stronger restoring effect at fixed mass.

questions.prompt: An experimenter changes an axial spring constant but keeps the transverse tension unchanged, then expects the transverse rate to follow the lecture’s thicker-spring row. What issue must be checked first?

options.text: Whether the block was made to move longitudinally as well, since transverse rate comparisons are meaningful only after motion is allowed in both directions together.
options.feedback: The demonstration can compare transverse systems directly. The issue is what changed the transverse restoring effect, not whether longitudinal motion was also enabled.

options.text: Whether the transverse displacement was drawn with the same maximum height, since equal drawing heights are what make two transverse stiffnesses comparable.
options.feedback: Display height can be enlarged independently of restoring stiffness. Matching a drawing scale does not establish the mechanical change.

options.text: Whether the change actually increased total restoring stiffness in the transverse direction, which in the demonstration depends on pre-tension and geometry.
options.feedback: The symbol K denotes total restoring stiffness in the direction of motion. The transverse model obtains it from pre-tension and geometry, so an axial change alone is not automatically the demonstrated transverse change.

options.text: Whether a different mass was used to accompany the axial change, since an unchanged mass prevents a transverse spring adjustment from affecting its timing.
options.feedback: Mass can remain fixed while effective restoring stiffness changes the rate. The missing check concerns the actual transverse restoring stiffness.

questions.answer: The symbol K denotes total restoring stiffness in the direction of motion. The transverse model obtains it from pre-tension and geometry, so an axial change alone is not automatically the demonstrated transverse change.
rubric: Distinguish axial spring constant from effective transverse restoring stiffness.
Use the demonstration’s pre-tension and geometry assumptions.
questions.topic: Effective stiffness depends on the motion direction

options.text: The relative rate ordering and frequency ratios remain the same, because a common slowdown changes each rate proportionally.

options.text: The higher modes become proportionally slower than the lower ones, so their displayed rate ordering reverses even though the same factor is used.

options.text: The equal slowdown makes the modes share one displayed frequency, since applying the same transformation removes their initial rate differences.

questions.answer: The source slows the motions uniformly for viewing. This preserves their relative rates while the Hz labels describe the unslowed physical frequencies.

questions.prompt: A learner traces a transverse string outline and claims that the air elements in the vocal-tract model must move along that same up-and-down path. Which correction fits the air demonstration?

options.text: The string outline is a time axis for each air element, so higher points represent later moments rather than a spatial pattern.
options.feedback: The analogy is between spatial mode patterns. An outline’s vertical position is not an elapsed-time coordinate.

options.text: The air elements follow the transverse outline, while the springs move longitudinally to keep the two directions dynamically separate.
options.feedback: The displayed air elements themselves move longitudinally along the tube.

options.text: The air elements move longitudinally along the tube; the comparison concerns related mode patterns, not identical directions of physical displacement.
options.feedback: The source explicitly represents air by masses moving along the tube. A transverse string can help reveal spatial mode structure without becoming the literal trajectory of each air element.

options.text: The air elements remain stationary while the whole tube moves transversely, so the visible spacing changes represent tube position rather than compression.
options.feedback: The source shows changing air-element spacing as those elements move and compress or rarefy.

questions.answer: The source explicitly represents air by masses moving along the tube. A transverse string can help reveal spatial mode structure without becoming the literal trajectory of each air element.

questions.prompt: The uniform-tube comparison has odd-multiple resonances, but the illustrated /i/ formants do not follow that simple ratio. Which explanation reconciles the two figures?

options.text: The first and second formant labels exchange their frequency order when a constriction appears, making the uniform ratio look different without changing a mode.
options.feedback: Formant order is not relabeled in this manner. The constriction changes resonance frequencies.

options.text: The /i/ labels must be source harmonics rather than formants, because a labeled resonance cannot depart from the uniform-tube frequency ratios.
options.feedback: The labels explicitly identify /i/ formants. The uniform assumption does not apply unchanged to the shaped tract.

options.text: The common 100 Hz source makes the vocal tract uniform, so any apparent resonance difference should be read as a change in recording amplitude.
options.feedback: Shared source spacing does not make the tract uniform or remove frequency differences in its filter.

options.text: The odd-multiple rule belongs to the ideal uniform reference; the /i/ constriction makes the tract nonuniform and changes its resonance pattern.
options.feedback: The corrected principles distinguish the ideal uniform fixed–free tube from a shaped vocal tract. Different constriction locations perturb the modes differently, so the uniform ratio is not imposed on each vowel.

questions.answer: The corrected principles distinguish the ideal uniform fixed–free tube from a shaped vocal tract. Different constriction locations perturb the modes differently, so the uniform ratio is not imposed on each vowel.
rubric: Identify uniformity as an assumption of the simple ratio.
Connect a nonuniform constriction with changed mode-specific resonances.
questions.topic: Uniform-tube assumptions and real vowel shapes

questions.prompt: One student places the illustrated /i/ constriction two-thirds of the way from the glottis toward the lips. Another places it one-third of the way back from the lips. How should those descriptions be evaluated?

options.text: They contradict because the distance to a constriction has to be numerically the same when measured from either endpoint.
options.feedback: Distances from opposite endpoints can have different fractional values.

options.text: They agree for a uniform tube, but a constricted /i/ tract requires a different conversion between fractions measured from opposite endpoints.
options.feedback: Both fractions describe portions of the same total tract length. Changing its cross-sectional uniformity does not alter that complementary distance relation.

options.text: They describe the distinct /i/ and /a/ locations, because any use of one-third refers to the back constriction regardless of the starting end.
options.feedback: One-third from the glottis and one-third from the lips are different locations. The reference end matters.

options.text: They can describe the same location, because they measure the remaining distance from opposite ends of the same tract.
options.feedback: The marker is two-thirds from the glottis and therefore one-third from the lips. A location statement must retain its reference end before it is compared with another description.

questions.answer: The marker is two-thirds from the glottis and therefore one-third from the lips. A location statement must retain its reference end before it is compared with another description.
rubric: Retain the endpoint from which the fraction is measured.
Recognize complementary descriptions of the same physical location.

questions.prompt: Relative to the uniform reference, a hypothetical constriction produces a lower F1 but a higher F2. Which local diagnosis agrees with the illustrated /i/ reasoning?

options.text: The mass effect dominates the first mode at the constriction, while local deformation makes the stiffness effect dominate the second mode.
options.feedback: The /i/ explanation links a downward first-mode shift to mass-dominated motion and an upward second-mode shift to stiffness-dominated compression. It infers different local sensitivities at the same position.

options.text: The added mass dominates both modes, with the increase in F2 showing a faster motion caused by the same extra moving inertia.
options.feedback: Increased mass lowers frequency in the stated comparison, so it does not explain the upward F2 shift.

options.text: The stiffness effect dominates the first mode, while mass dominates the second, because increased stiffness is the cause of a lower first resonance.
options.feedback: This reverses the physical directions and the illustrated local diagnosis.

options.text: The stiffness effect dominates both modes, with the downward F1 shift showing that compression and frequency change in opposite directions.
options.feedback: Increased effective stiffness raises frequency under fixed-mass comparison, not lowers it.

questions.answer: The /i/ explanation links a downward first-mode shift to mass-dominated motion and an upward second-mode shift to stiffness-dominated compression. It infers different local sensitivities at the same position.
rubric: Infer mass dominance from the first downward shift.
Infer stiffness dominance from the second upward shift.

questions.prompt: In the illustrated /u/ model, imagine undoing just the added free-end mass loading while keeping the reference stiffness and other conditions unchanged. What directional change is predicted relative to the loaded case?

options.text: Both first-mode and second-mode frequencies should rise toward their unloaded reference values, reversing the demonstrated mass-loading effect.
options.feedback: The illustrated added mass lowers both frequencies because both modes move strongly near the lips. Removing that addition under the stated fixed conditions reverses those dominant shifts.

options.text: Their rates should stay at the loaded values, because a local mass change alters the drawing’s size but not the resonances of a moving air system.
options.feedback: The source attributes the downward shifts to the local added mass, so reversing that change matters.

options.text: The first should rise and the second fall, because removing a shared mass addition converts the second mode’s free end into a compression node.
options.feedback: Removing the stated mass addition does not impose that new boundary condition or the claimed opposite direction.

options.text: Both frequencies should fall farther, because removing mass strengthens the same inertial effect that lowered them in the loaded comparison.
options.feedback: Removing mass reverses the added-inertia effect rather than strengthening it.

questions.answer: The illustrated added mass lowers both frequencies because both modes move strongly near the lips. Removing that addition under the stated fixed conditions reverses those dominant shifts.
rubric: Keep stiffness and the comparison conditions fixed.
Reverse the demonstrated downward mass-loading shifts.

questions.prompt: Two illustrated output spectra have the same harmonic frequencies, and every line in the second is scaled taller by the same proportion. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The number of formants has increased, because strengthening each harmonic adds a separate resonance at the corresponding source frequency.
options.feedback: Stronger source components do not each become new tract resonances.

options.text: The vowel filter has shifted each resonance upward, because taller spectral lines represent higher frequencies even when their horizontal positions stay fixed.
options.feedback: Height is amplitude, while frequency is horizontal position. A common scaling does not establish shifted resonances.

options.text: The overall amplitude has changed, but this alone does not show a changed vowel filter because the relative-height envelope has not been reshaped.
options.feedback: The source–filter examples distinguish frequency spacing from the pattern of relative amplitudes. A common gain changes size without providing evidence for a different pattern of resonance emphasis.

options.text: The fundamental frequency has increased, because a taller source comb indicates a shorter time between repetitions even when its spacing is unchanged.
options.feedback: Amplitude height is not harmonic spacing or repetition rate.

questions.answer: The source–filter examples distinguish frequency spacing from the pattern of relative amplitudes. A common gain changes size without providing evidence for a different pattern of resonance emphasis.
rubric: Distinguish overall amplitude scaling from a relative-height pattern.
Avoid inferring changed F0 or resonance locations from height alone.
questions.topic: Uniform amplitude change versus filter reshaping

questions.prompt: The /a/ filter labels F1 at 750 Hz while the source harmonics remain 100 Hz apart. How can the figure represent that formant without placing a harmonic exactly at 750 Hz?

options.text: The source fundamental should be relabeled 750 Hz, because a first formant defines the lowest source component in the filtered signal.
options.feedback: F1 and F0 have different roles. The source comb remains 100 Hz-spaced.

options.text: The resonance can strengthen nearby source components around 700 and 800 Hz, with their heights sampling an envelope whose peak lies between them.
options.feedback: A formant is a filter resonance, not a requirement that the source contain a component at that exact frequency. The source explicitly illustrates the 750 Hz resonance between neighboring harmonics.

options.text: The F1 label should be moved to the nearest tallest harmonic, because the resonance position is defined by the grid of available source components.
options.feedback: A resonance can lie between components; a sampled peak does not define the exact filter resonance.

options.text: The filter should create a new 750 Hz harmonic and discard its neighbors, because a resonance cannot be represented by amplitudes at adjacent frequencies.
options.feedback: The illustration preserves source harmonic positions and shapes their heights near the resonance.

questions.answer: A formant is a filter resonance, not a requirement that the source contain a component at that exact frequency. The source explicitly illustrates the 750 Hz resonance between neighboring harmonics.
rubric: Separate a filter resonance from an exact source component.
Explain sampling of the envelope by nearby harmonics.

questions.prompt: The schematic schwa and /a/ examples share an F4 label of 3500 Hz but differ in lower formants. What does their shared F4 establish?

options.text: The two examples have equivalent vocal-tract filters, because matching the highest labeled resonance fixes the positions of the lower three.
options.feedback: The displayed lower formants explicitly differ despite matching F4.

options.text: One illustrated resonance is shared; it does not make the full filters or vowels equivalent when the remaining resonance pattern differs.
options.feedback: The schwa and /a/ figures differ in their lower formant labels and envelopes despite sharing this F4 value. A single matched resonance does not specify the whole filter.

options.text: The shared value identifies their source fundamental as 3500 Hz, with the lower groups representing subharmonics of that common source.
options.feedback: The label is F4, a tract formant, while the source is shown with 100 Hz harmonic spacing.

options.text: The two examples must have different source spacings to explain the lower-formant differences, even though the source panels display the same comb.
options.feedback: Different filters can shape one shared source; changing source spacing is not required.

questions.answer: The schwa and /a/ figures differ in their lower formant labels and envelopes despite sharing this F4 value. A single matched resonance does not specify the whole filter.
rubric: Interpret a shared formant as a partial match.
Use the full resonance pattern rather than one label.
questions.topic: Shared higher formant and vowel identity

questions.prompt: Under the illustrated grayscale key, a band stays at the same vertical frequency but becomes darker as time advances. What change is represented?

options.text: The frequency increases while amplitude remains fixed, because darker ink indicates a higher point on the frequency axis.
options.feedback: Frequency would require a vertical-position change. Darkness encodes amplitude here.

options.text: The source pitch decreases, because a darker mark is the display’s way of representing a larger gap between adjacent harmonics.
options.feedback: A band’s darkness does not measure harmonic spacing or source pitch.

options.text: The band’s duration increases, because darker marks represent longer persistence of a sound when the vertical frequency position stays fixed.
options.feedback: The legend maps darkness to amplitude. Duration follows horizontal extent or elapsed time, rather than the shade of a mark.

options.text: Amplitude at that frequency increases while its frequency position remains unchanged in the display.
options.feedback: The source maps amplitude to darkness and frequency to vertical position. A change in one encoding does not require a change in the other.

questions.answer: The source maps amplitude to darkness and frequency to vertical position. A change in one encoding does not require a change in the other.
rubric: Read darkness using the supplied amplitude key.
Keep frequency position distinct from amplitude.

questions.prompt: Suppose the same short-time spectra are placed on a spectrogram in reverse time order without changing any individual spectrum. Which property changes?

options.text: The stronger amplitudes in each slice become weaker, because moving a slice to a different horizontal position reverses the darkness key.
options.feedback: Horizontal ordering and amplitude encoding are different operations.

options.text: The direction of the displayed vowel transition reverses, while each individual time slice retains its frequency–amplitude information.
options.feedback: A spectrogram preserves the order of successive spectra. Reversing that order reverses the trajectory through time but does not alter the contents of a particular spectrum.

options.text: The harmonic frequencies inside each original slice are reversed in sign, because time reversal of the display exchanges frequency and amplitude axes.
options.feedback: Reordering slices does not exchange their axes or change their recorded component values.

options.text: The formant bands remain in the same temporal sequence, because a spectrogram is an average spectrum that discards ordering before it is drawn.
options.feedback: The source explicitly stacks spectra over time, preserving their order.

questions.answer: A spectrogram preserves the order of successive spectra. Reversing that order reverses the trajectory through time but does not alter the contents of a particular spectrum.
rubric: Recognize the time-order information supplied by stacking.
Separate reordering slices from changing their contents.

questions.prompt: You want to test whether wider source spacing obscures formants without changing the filter itself. Which comparison isolates that issue most directly?

options.text: Hold the illustrated resonance envelope fixed, vary the source harmonic spacing, and compare how the available line heights reveal that same envelope.
options.feedback: The source comparison changes F0 while holding the filter fixed. This isolates the density of harmonic samples rather than combining pitch differences with new resonance locations.

options.text: Compare different vowels and different source pitches together, attributing any difference in visible bands to pitch without tracking the changed resonances.
options.feedback: Changing both source and filter confounds the explanation of the visible bands.

options.text: Hold the source spacing fixed but move the resonance peaks, using the resulting envelope difference as evidence that the source samples became sparser.
options.feedback: That manipulates the filter rather than source sampling density.

options.text: Compare the total amplitudes of two recordings without examining their harmonic positions, treating the louder one as the more densely sampled filter.
options.feedback: Overall amplitude does not measure the spacing of the available harmonic samples.

questions.answer: The source comparison changes F0 while holding the filter fixed. This isolates the density of harmonic samples rather than combining pitch differences with new resonance locations.
rubric: Hold filter conditions fixed.
Vary harmonic spacing and inspect how it samples the envelope.

questions.prompt: In a high-F0 spectrum, one strong harmonic appears near a resonance region but few neighbors sample the envelope. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The strong harmonic’s frequency directly establishes the exact formant, because high F0 makes a sample and its underlying resonance the same physical quantity.
options.feedback: Wider spacing reduces evidence about the envelope rather than making a component identical to a resonance.

options.text: The filter has lost the neighboring formants, because the lack of nearby source components means those resonance mechanisms no longer exist in the tract.
options.feedback: A sparse source can leave resonances poorly sampled without removing them from the filter.

options.text: The exact formant location is less securely revealed by that isolated line; its frequency is a sample of the filter response rather than proof of the envelope’s peak.
options.feedback: Sparse harmonics can obscure the resonance envelope. A strong available sample can lie near a formant without locating the resonance exactly or proving that other resonances are absent.

options.text: The strong line establishes a lower F0 than the dense-source example, because fewer neighboring components indicate more closely spaced repetitions.
options.feedback: Fewer harmonics in a fixed frequency region reflect wider spacing and higher F0 in the comparison.

questions.answer: Sparse harmonics can obscure the resonance envelope. A strong available sample can lie near a formant without locating the resonance exactly or proving that other resonances are absent.
rubric: Treat an isolated harmonic as a sample rather than an exact resonance measurement.
